chapter_theme: Not offending the great: to slight those with real power is to call down one's own ruin, and no wealth, fort or ally protects against them. Who the great are is the key question, and the verses themselves mostly leave it open.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the great into two: kings who can destroy (893-895) and ascetics whose anger can do anything (896-900). Manakkudavar also has ascetics in view, but the verses don't name them. Kalaignar reads them throughout as worthy or capable people, with no curses.

891.reading: Not slighting the power of those able to act is the highest of all safeguards for those who guard themselves.
891.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes a large claim from this: fort, army, wealth and friends can all be undone by such people, so this safeguard outranks them. It closes a stretch of chapters that were all about those other safeguards.

892.reading: Going on without regard for the great will, through the great, bring ills that do not leave.
892.nuance: The grammar makes the conduct itself the agent, and the great are only the instrument. Parimelazhagar says this was meant to show people do it to themselves. He has the king as the one at fault, whereas Manakkudavar has a person failing to honour sages.

893.reading: If you want to be ruined, don't listen, and commit a fault against those able to destroy.
893.nuance: A piece of grim irony, phrased as an instruction. The commentators differ on what isn't listened to: Parimelazhagar means the treatises on policy, and Manakkudavar means the great themselves. His Purananuru citation makes such kings swifter than Death, who at least waits for the time.

894.reading: For those who can't do harm to those who can is like beckoning Death with the hand.
894.nuance: The word is விளி, to call, so the gesture does it. Parimelazhagar adds that Death would have come anyway, so the action only brings it sooner, and that the hand gesture itself carries a scornful tone.

895.reading: Wherever they go, they won't exist anywhere, those who've drawn the anger of a king of fierce might.
895.nuance: Parimelazhagar is shrewdly political: other kings won't shelter the fugitive and may kill him to win favour or his goods. The verse's point is not the king's reach but what everyone around him will do because of it.

896.reading: Even if burned by fire, there can be survival; those who go on offending the great will not survive.

positions.position: The great are ascetics, whose wrath strikes at the life itself in an instant where fire only reaches the body first.
positions.quote: தவத்தாற் பெரியாரைப் பிழைத்து ஒழுகுவார், எவ்வாற்றானும் உயிருய்யார்.

positions.position: The great are sages, with the same conclusion.
The great are simply those mighty in capacity, with no asceticism involved.
positions.quote: ஆற்றல் மிகுந்த பெரியோரிடம் தவறிழைப்போர் தப்பிப் பிழைப்பது முடியாது.

897.reading: What are a fully appointed life and lofty wealth, if worthy ones of great stature are angered?
897.nuance: Parimelazhagar says தகை means greatness that can curse and bless. Note his remark that செறின் implies they usually don't get angry, which holds for the verses after this. The verse's question doesn't state a mechanism, while he describes royal wealth burning up in a moment.

898.reading: If hill-like people are held low or themselves turn to bringing low, those who seemed to stand forever will vanish from earth with their line.
898.nuance: நின்றன்னார், those who 'seem to stand', and குன்றன்னார், those who 'are like hills': the verse compares two kinds of standing. குன்ற is also a verbal pun on the hill.

positions.position: குன்ற மதித்தல் is what the hill-like ascetics do, resolving on someone's ruin, and the rich die with their kin at once.
It is done to them: someone thinks little of those who are great as hills.

899.reading: If those of exalted resolve flare up, even the வேந்தன் breaks midway and loses his kingship.
899.nuance: ஏந்திய கொள்கை and வேந்தன் carry all the weight in this verse, and the disagreement could hardly be wider, from gods and vows to politics.

positions.position: The வேந்தன் is Indra, himself toppled by ascetics of great vows, with Nahusha's fall from Indra's seat through Agastya's anger in mind.
positions.quote: அவராற்றலான் இந்திரனும் இடைய தன் பதம் இழந்து கெடும்.

positions.position: It is also Indra, who loses his realm, and this is a loss of wealth.
positions.quote: உயர்ந்த கோட்பாட்டையுடையார் வெகுள்வராயின், இந்திரனும் இடையிலே இற்றுத் தன்னரசு இழக்கும்

positions.position: Those with firm principles rise up and a repressive regime collapses, with no god or vow in it.

900.reading: Even those with overwhelming support will not survive if those of supreme distinction are angered.
900.nuance: சார்பு gets a precise list from Parimelazhagar: fort, army, wealth, friends, which are the chapters just passed through. His example is the burning of the three cities. The verse's own சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் doesn't specify asceticism or any cause.

links.note: 781 says no guard is as hard to get past as friendship. 891 says not slighting the able outranks every safeguard. Parimelazhagar lists friendship among those it outranks, so a long section that praised friendship and forts closes by ranking something above them.

Death personified, twice. In 765 an army stands united when Death comes raging. In 894 the fool waves Death over with his own hand. The difference between courage and folly is not whether one faces Death, but whether one sent the invitation.

Both rank fire below something else: in 129 the burn from fire heals and the burn of the tongue doesn't, and in 896 one may survive the fire but not offence given to the great. Fire is the Kural's standard for what is bad but survivable.

29 calls the great those who have climbed a hill of virtue, whose anger can't be withstood even for a moment. 898 calls them hill-like, and 896-897 in Parimelazhagar's reading have the same instant destruction. Chapter 90 develops what chapter 3 states about the renunciant, in the political book.

25 calls Indra sufficient witness to the power of the one who controls the senses. Parimelazhagar makes 899's வேந்தன் Indra as well. The Kural itself only names Indra in 25, so the connection depends on his gloss.

864 says one who doesn't let go of anger is easy prey for anyone. 899 makes the anger of the exalted able to bring down a king. Anger is weakness or supreme power depending on who has it, and 306 warns that it burns the one who has it.

source_issues: 896: Parimelazhagar's comment cites '(குறள் -6)' for the point about wrath lasting a moment, but that wording matches 29. This looks like a citation error.
899: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is scrambled (இடை வேந்த முரிந்து) and the quote used has a likely misprint (இடைய for இடையே).
